content: 1. A clinical trial conducted in Tanzania evaluated the effectiveness of quadruple-fortified salt in improving nutritional outcomes. (2020) 2. A study in Mali assessed the management of children with moderate acute malnutrition, focusing on nutritional interventions and their outcomes. (2011) 3. Research on a new infant cereal examined its acceptability, tolerance, satiety, and prebiotic effects, highlighting its potential benefits for infant nutrition. (2017) 4. In Haitian women and preschool children, iron absorption from wheat flour meals fortified with sodium iron EDTA was found to be higher than from meals fortified with ferrous fumarate. Additionally, the presence of Helicobacter pylori infection in children did not affect iron absorption. (2017) 5. A study in Botswana tested a multi-nutrient fortified beverage in children, exploring its impact on nutritional status and growth. (2002) 6. Research in Myanmar investigated the effects of iron supplementation, with or without optimized complementary feeding recommendations, on the micronutrient status and growth of children aged 1–2 years. (2015) 7. A randomized clinical trial in breastfed term infants demonstrated that feeding baby food containing DHA-enriched egg yolk accelerated the maturation of visual acuity. (2004) 8. A study in Niger evaluated the impact of ready-to-use therapeutic food supplementation on the nutritional status, mortality, and morbidity of children aged 6–60 months. (2008) 9. A trial in Kenya assessed the acceptability of new formulations of corn-soy blends and lipid-based nutrient supplements for treating moderate acute malnutrition in children. (2015) 10. Research in Kenya found that iron fortification of wheat flour with NaFeEDTA improved iron absorption in children, with no adverse effects from Helicobacter pylori infection. (2015) 11. A study in Malawi compared the effects of fortified spreads and corn-soy blends on recovery rates in moderately wasted children, finding higher recovery rates with fortified spreads. (2009) 12. A trial in Zambia demonstrated that multiple micronutrient supplementation using Spirulina platensis positively influenced growth, morbidity, and motor development in infants. (2019) 13. A study in Senegal explored the effects of early infant food supplementation on maternal weight loss, breastfeeding duration, and infant growth. (2006) 14. Research in Kenya showed that maize porridge enriched with a micronutrient powder containing low-dose iron as NaFeEDTA reduced anemia and iron deficiency in preschool children. (2012) 15. A randomized controlled trial in Tanzania found that processed complementary food did not improve growth or hemoglobin status in infants aged 6–12 months. (2004) 16. A study in Sierra Leone demonstrated that severe and moderate acute malnutrition could be successfully managed using an integrated protocol. (2015) 17. Research in Ethiopia assessed the effects of iodized salt on cognitive development in children, highlighting its potential benefits. (2014) 18. A study in Uganda evaluated the effectiveness of nutritional supplementation in preventing malnutrition in children with infections. (2012) 19. A trial in Zambia found that dietary diversity at six months of age was associated with subsequent growth and mediated the effect of maternal education on infant growth. (2014) 20. A study in Mexico evaluated the sensory acceptability of nutritional supplements enriched with different forms of iron in rural communities. (2008) 21. Research in Kenya demonstrated that maize porridge fortified with amaranth grain or micronutrient powder containing NaFeEDTA improved iron intake and status in children. (2013) 22. A study in Malawi found that home-based therapy for severe malnutrition using ready-to-use food was effective in improving recovery rates. (2004) 23. A trial in Kenya showed that adding amylase to fortified blended foods increased energy and nutrient intake in children aged 12–35 months. (2018) 24. A study in Kenya demonstrated that locally produced complementary foods improved fat-free mass, linear growth, and iron status in infants. (2019) 25. Research in Kenya found that meat as a first complementary food for breastfed infants was feasible and improved zinc intake and status. (2006) 26. A study in Burkina Faso evaluated the acceptability of improved supplementary foods for treating moderate acute malnutrition using a mixed-method approach. (2016) 27. A trial in Malawi found that an energy-dense complementary food modestly increased weight gain compared to fortified porridge in children aged 6–18 months. (2008) 28. A study in Kenya demonstrated that dietary iron intake was positively associated with hemoglobin concentration during infancy but not during the second year of life. (2004) 29.
